responses.title: Task 1: Critiques of Aid
responses.prompt:
Please provide a brief response to the challenge:
"Of the critiques made against international humanitarianism in general, which do you think is the most persuasive? To what degree is that critique contextually specific or universally generalisable? An open goal to start the module! A lot has and is being said about humanitarianism. Which do you think is fair and appropriate and where is the local environment and context distorting the wider position?"
responses.responseText:
The critique I find most persuasive is the tension between humanitarian relief and longer-term development. Captured in the analogy that emergency services do not operate independently of a wider healthcare system, it is presented as an artificial divide that makes little sense to crisis-affected populations for whom survival and longer-term needs are inseparable (Levine and Barnett, cited in Anyangwe, 2015).

Humanitarian assistance sustaining basic needs without corresponding to system-level stability is particularly visible in protracted crises such as South Sudan, effectively substituting for, rather than strengthening, state capacity (Donini, 2010). MSF’s reflections also note that while its programmes deliver clear medical impact, they may also inadvertently displace local systems and create chronic dependency in partnerships, reinforcing its caution about taking on a broader development role (Abu-Sada, 2012).

However, addressing this by collapsing the distinction between relief and development intersects with broader critiques of humanitarianism as embedded in global power structures, particularly where external actors shape national systems (Donini, 2010), and risks blurring core principles such as neutrality and independence as humanitarian actors become more embedded in state or political processes (Leader, 1998).

Rather than a context-specific or universally generalisable critique, I view this as an inherent, recurring structural tension within humanitarian action that consistently emerges across contexts. While much of the literature is dated, recent analysis shows that rigid funding models, institutional competition and misaligned economic incentives continue to fragment humanitarian responses (Lilly and Pearson, 2025). Anyangwe (2015) argues that addressing such tensions through more coordinated, long-term approaches involves incremental change over longer time horizons.
bibliography: Abu-Sada, C. (ed.) (2012) In the Eyes of Others: How People in Crises Perceive Humanitarian Aid. New York: Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF-USA).

Anyangwe, E. (2015) ‘Is it time to rethink the divide between humanitarian and development funding?’, The Guardian, 4 December. Available at: https://www.theguardian.com/global-development-professionals-network/2015/dec/04/is-it-time-to-rethink-the-divide-between-humanitarian-and-development-funding (Accessed: 4 April 2026).
Donini, A. (2010) ‘The far side: the meta functions of humanitarianism in a globalised world’, Disasters, 34(S2), pp. S220–S237.
Leader, N. (1998) ‘Proliferating principles; or how to sup with the devil without getting eaten’, Disasters, 22(4), pp. 288–308.

Lilly, D. and Pearson, M. (2025) ‘Change the economic incentives to reform the humanitarian system’, LSE Activism, Influence and Change Blog, 27 October. Available at https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/activism-influence-change/2025/10/27/change-the-economic-incentives-to-reform-the-humanitarian-system/ (Accessed: 4 April 2026).

responses.title: Task 2: Quality initiatives and competency frameworks
responses.prompt:
Please respond to the following:
"If you use any of the quality initiatives discussed in the materials, how and in what ways do you employ them?
Consider your own experience in this field and how the issue of performance and professionalisation has shaped your thoughts and actions. In this light, briefly review the Core Humanitarian Competencies Framework and provide an evaluation of how well the document content reflects your concept of the most fundamental capabilities. Do you agree all the aspects of what appears to have become the consensus?"
Styles and approaches to programming and the influence of what might be considered to be macro-trends will be explored during this week.
responses.responseText:
In my role, I draw on knowledge and learning approaches outlined by Ramalingam (2006), particularly the idea that tools only improve performance when supported by appropriate processes, relationships, and governance. I apply this by designing information environments, shared digital platforms and cultural practices that enable knowledge to flow across teams rather than remain siloed to improve access to information, and support decision-making and organisational learning. This aligns with standards such as the Core Humanitarian Standard, which defines quality through commitments to relevant, timely assistance and continuous learning and improvement (CHS Alliance, 2014).

Competencies related to collaboration, coordination, and information sharing - such as working accountably, developing collaborative relationships, and using appropriate communication channels (ALNAP, 2012) - partially address what Walker and Russ (2010) describe as limited coordination and the absence of a shared understanding of professional competence. In practice, this contributes to fragmentation, duplicated work, poor information visibility, and inefficient decision-making, with gaps in information management capacity (Ramalingam, 2006) and limited access to training (O’Dempsey, 2012) further constraining effectiveness. This was evident in the 2010 Haiti earthquake, where parallel coordination structures and weak information sharing led to duplicated assessments and gaps in service delivery (James, 2016).

I therefore view the framework as a system-aligned operational language rather than a true consensus on fundamental capabilities, as its implementation is shaped by organisational contexts. Walker and Russ (2010) highlight the historical fragmentation of the sector and the challenges of defining shared professional knowledge and defining “fundamental” capabilities also remains context-dependent, as humanitarian action spans diverse environments and is embedded in political and social dynamics (Donini, 2010). Participation in defining standards is uneven, meaning apparent consensus may reflect predominantly Western institutional perspectives (O’Dempsey, 2012).

While the Core Humanitarian Competencies Framework captures key behavioural capabilities such as communication, teamwork, and ethical practice (ALNAP, 2012), it does not explicitly address how power shapes knowledge flows. As Ramalingam (2006) and Donini (2010) show, information is often tied to authority, reinforcing a “knowledge is power” dynamic that can limit collaboration and constrain the sharing of tacit, experiential and locallised knowledge. Abu-Sada (2012) illustrates this in Afghanistan, where humanitarian actors were disconnected from local realities, while James (2016) shows how professionalisation can widen gaps between international and local expertise. In my experience, similar resistance emerges when shifting toward shared knowledge systems, suggesting that many core capabilities are relational and systemic rather than fully captured through behavioural competencies.

The framework may also benefit from modernisation in increasingly digital environments. A lack of digital skills limits the effective use of technology (Centre for Humanitarian Action, n.d.), while unequal access to infrastructure shapes participation in digital systems (ITU, 2024). Although managerial competencies include enabling others and promoting the use of technology , they could go further to include active oversight of digital systems - including understanding their risks, limitations, and resource requirements. Without this, the framework risks treating technology as a tool to be encouraged rather than a system to be actively managed, limiting its applicability in contemporary, data-driven operations.

Looking to other sectors, I am reminded of my experience studying human performance competency frameworks at the International Space University, particularly around resilience in extreme environments and operating under safety constraints. While the Core Humanitarian Competencies Framework frames resilience through behaviours such as remaining focused, adapting calmly, and recognising stress (ALNAP, 2012), NASA defines it through observable markers such as identifying stress early and applying countermeasures before it affects task execution (Schmidt, 2008), treating resilience as managing performance degradation rather than maintaining composure, which risks overestimating effectiveness in high-pressure environments.

responses.title: Task 1: Project Management capability
responses.prompt:
Please take this short assessment and consider the output and where the focus of your learning might need to be:
This is a self-test. You can reflect upon it in the Discussion Board if you wish, but this is not required.
responses.responseText:
I scored 79 on the assessment, which positioned me as an "accomplished" project manager and encouraged me to keep developing others while reflecting on my own practice.

My project management experience includes leading complex, multi-market projects across large organisations (for example for Meta and Google), and currently at MSF leading a multi-workstream, interdisciplinary transformation spanning systems, governance, and ways of working. This has involved combining quantitative data with ethnographic and qualitative nuance to build context-aware behavioural models and indicators that inform product, strategy, and resource decisions. This reflects a design-led approach: structuring messy problems into something teams can act on. shaping what they build, test, and scale, and iterating through experimentation alongside broader plans, rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all framework across the project lifecycle. It also highlights the challenge of translating complex human realities into indicators that actually work (for example, converting cultural, behavioural, and emotional dynamics into precise, system-ready metrics for algorithmic decision-making), while keeping requirements and outputs clear and usable across stakeholders, from leadership to technical and operational staff.

The MindTools quiz, however, assumes a more linear, control-oriented model with clear scope, upfront planning, and individual accountability. I share Colleen’s experience of finding some questions difficult to answer despite having project experience, as they don’t reflect environments where ownership is distributed, coordination is actively facilitated, and planning evolves through continuous experimentation and feedback. My key learning is applying this balance in humanitarian contexts, where decisions are made with incomplete data, shifting conditions, and coordination constraints. The focus for me is translating a design-led, adaptive approach into clearer decision points, ownership, and context-aware implementation and indicators - while recognising these will never fully align with predefined models and must remain flexible and responsible to realities on the ground in practice.
bibliography: Brown, T. (2008) ‘Design thinking’, Harvard Business Review, 86(6), pp. 84–92.

responses.title: Task 2: Review and Analyse Project Management
responses.prompt:
Please put your thoughts in the Discussion Board on the following issues:
Review the online project management tools and discuss their utility.
Discuss your experience of project management tools that are or are not being used in your work environment and how they have improved or constrained your work and that of your organisation.
responses.responseText:
Since this task begins with tools rather than the conditions that make them meaningful, it is important to situation them within the critiques of project management, particularly where projects are often treated as technical problems solved through methods and platforms while overlooking their purpose, value, and relationship to wider organisational systems (Söderlund, 2004). In my experience, a jobs-to-be-done perspective within design thinking can address this by defining the progress required to deliver value before selecting solutions, reframing tools as means rather than the end, “hired” to enable change rather than treated as starting points (Christensen et al., 2016). This is particularly relevant in humanitarian contexts, where projects sit within broader intervention systems linking short-term delivery to longer-term social and operational dynamics (James, 2017).

As incomplete and context-dependent data can be misinterpreted and hinder effective performance and indicator monitoring (Malteser International, 2009), the priority is ensuring that ground-level inputs are accurately translated into decision-making rather than focusing on the tool itself. When translated into indicators, dashboards, or AI-assisted outputs, these realities are necessarily simplified, meaning representation is shaped by what can be formalised rather than the full complexity of context; this is reinforced by Anthropic’s findings that language models can generate plausible yet unfaithful explanations that do not fully reflect their underlying reasoning processes (Anthropic, 2025). Simpler tools such as Excel, shared documents, whiteboards, or paper can therefore remain valuable in capturing capturing nuance, enabling co-creation, and supporting diverse input gathering, particularly in low-connectivity settings where in-person coordination remains central. In my experience, while organisational tools such as Monday (now transitioning to Asana for cost and ethical reasons) are required for reporting and oversight, teams often rely more on Excel for its flexibility in structuring and adapting data, alongside Microsoft Loop for its integration with everyday project workflows such as Teams, meetings, and messaging, as well as lightweight planning and Kanban-style coordination without needing separate tools like Trello. A further constraint I experience is the proliferation of fragmented tool ecosystems and third-party tools outside restricted organisational environments like Microsoft, introducing duplication, parallel repositories, record management challenges, and governance risks, including unclear ownership when task-based tools are used permanent "sources of truth" and data exposure through API integrations.

Ultimately, tools should support coordination and consistency rather than become proxies for control or add unnecessary cognitive burden. Given the limits of working memory (Cowan, 2019), constant context-switching and complex or unintuitive navigation reduce attention and decision quality (Sweller, 2011), increasing the risk of human error in high-pressure environments. In such contexts, failure is less about which tool was used, and more about breakdowns in communication, attention, and execution (Ancel and Shih, 2012; Shively, 2013), meaning even simple tools like checklists are only effective when they reinforce shared understanding and disciplined information flow rather than replace them (Gawande, 2007).
bibliography: Ancel, E. and Shih, A.T. (2012) The analysis of the contribution of human factors to in-flight loss of control accidents. NASA.

responses.title: Task 1
responses.prompt:
Using the psychometric assessment tools linked to Session 3 as a starting point, use the discussion board to answer these questions:
To what degree do your values align with what you are currently doing?
Are there changes you might undertake to bring them into closer alignment?
What could be the result?
responses.responseText:
Like others here, I approach psychometric assessments with caution, given their limited ability to capture my context and consistency since I've taken them several times over my career and receive different results each time. With that caveat, the identification of self-direction, universalism and hedonism broadly reflects how I approach my work, but does not fully capture it. For example, my 4-year strategy emphasises accessibility, collaboration, integrity and user-centricity as guiding values, aligning with a servant leadership orientation focused on meeting the needs of others (Spears, 2005), yet not fully reflected in the assessment.

In practice, self-direction is reflected in the autonomy required to lead information and knowledge management and digital transformation, while universalism is evident in my focus on equitable access and improving usability for staff and end users. In this context, influence relies less on formal authority and more on recognised expertise. This also reflects how I exercised leadership earlier in my career as an individual contributor, assuming leadership in shaping business strategy and direction without formal responsibility for managing people.

The assessment’s lower prioritisation of conformity, tradition and power helps explain tensions I experience when driving change in bureaucratic, change-resistant IT environments, where structural barriers, including the underrepresentation of women in ICT decision-making roles, shape influence and authority (United Nations, 2005; Buchanan-Smith, M. and Scriven, K, 2011), highlighting the gap between my values and the context in which they are applied.

To strengthen alignment, I would shift from primarily driving change through data and individual expertise towards more deliberate consensus-building and shared ownership. While self-direction supports vision-setting, it can underemphasise stakeholder alignment in complex humanitarian systems, where leadership depends on building collective ownership around a shared direction (Buchanan-Smith, M. and Scriven, K, 2011). Creating space for others to shape solutions, even where this slows delivery, would better translate these values into practice, converting resistance into engagement and increasing the likelihood that change is sustained.
bibliography: Buchanan-Smith, M. and Scriven, K. (2011) Leadership in action: Leading effectively in humanitarian operations. London: ALNAP/ODI.
Spears, L.C. (2005) The understanding and practice of servant-leadership. Servant Leadership Research Roundtable, Regent University, August.

Pittenger, D.J. (2005) ‘Cautionary comments regarding the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator’, Consulting Psychology Journal: Practice and Research, 57(3), pp. 210–221.

responses.title: Task 2
responses.prompt:
Pick a leader that you admire and/or who inspires you. It may be someone you know personally or a publicly known figure.
Who are they and what is their role? (If it’s someone you know personally, you don’t have to use their name)
What traits/characteristics/competencies do they have that make them effective leaders?
What do they do that makes them effective leaders?
responses.responseText:
I most admire a former academic teacher in life sciences and cognitive psychology whose leadership was grounded in analytical decision-making under uncertainty, structuring how complex problems were interpreted, evaluated, and acted upon.

Their effectiveness derived from disciplined sensemaking and judgement. They consistently decomposed ambiguous situations into underlying variables often rooted in attitudes and beliefs, distinguishing between perceived risk and actual risk (Slovic, 2000), separating emotional reactions from empirical evidence (Kahneman, 2011), and identifying how prior assumptions were shaping interpretation (Korteling et al., 2023), enabling them to assess competing interpretations and guide decisions without relying on complete information. A central competency was cognitive and emotional regulation, evident in their willingness to admit mistakes, avoid premature conclusions, and actively de-escalate situations where others tended to catastrophise, allowing the team to focus on what mattered in the moment rather than what might happen in the future, creating space for rational decision-making.

Their approach reflected the principle that responses are mediated by interpretation and beliefs rather than events themselves, shaping behavioural outcomes under stress (Vîslă et al., 2016). In high-risk team environments, this better enables consistent decision quality and reduces escalatory responses within the group (Helmreich, 1987), which had a visible effect on those who worked with them.

These characteristics reflect authentic leadership, particularly balanced processing and self-awareness emphasising objective evaluation before action (Avolio et al., 2009), aligning with leadership requiring direction and coordination under uncertainty (Buchanan-Smith and Scriven, 2011) and clear intent under significant risk (Kolditz, 2007), supporting disciplined and coordinated action under pressure.
bibliography: Avolio, B.J., Walumbwa, F.O. and Weber, T.J. (2009) ‘Leadership: Current theories, research, and future directions’, Annual Review of Psychology, 60, pp. 421–449.
Buchanan-Smith, M. and Scriven, K. (2011) Leadership in action: Leading effectively in humanitarian operations. London: ALNAP/ODI.

responses.title: Task 1: Leadership style
responses.prompt:
Reflect on the assigned reading and supporting materials.
Pick a theme or idea that has particular resonance for you (e.g. Schein’s three cultures or Sinek’s theory about great leadership) and talk about its application to your professional work.
responses.responseText:
A key theme that resonates is the limitation of transformational leadership when applied in complex organisational systems. Transformational leadership emphasises vision, motivation, and alignment around collective goals (Bass and Riggio, 2006). It operates through mechanisms such as inspirational motivation and intellectual stimulation, encouraging followers to move beyond individual interests toward shared purpose . This reflects my approach in leading a cross-organisational information management transformation, where I prioritised engagement and shared direction.

However, in practice, vision did not produce alignment. Teams interpreted the same direction through different professional logics and priorities. Schein’s (1996) concept of distinct organisational cultures explains this divergence, where actors operate from incompatible underlying assumptions. Situational leadership, which emphasises adapting leadership style to follower readiness, partially addresses variability. However, it assumes that alignment can be achieved primarily through behavioural adjustment. Empirical critiques challenge this assumption, highlighting conceptual ambiguity and limited predictive validity in the model (Meirovich and Gu, 2015). In this context, differences in interpretation were not simply a function of capability or motivation, but reflected deeper structural and cultural conditions shaping how teams understood and acted on the same directive.

My experience aligns with followership theory, where leadership outcomes are co-produced rather than leader-driven (Uhl-Bien et al., 2014). Effectiveness depended less on motivation and more on aligning underlying assumptions and structural conditions. Transformational leadership generated direction, but without shared interpretation and system coherence, it did not translate into coordinated action.
bibliography: Bass, B.M. and Riggio, R.E. (2006) Transformational Leadership. 2nd edn. Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
Meirovich, G. and Gu, J. (2015) ‘Empirical and theoretical validity of Hersey–Blanchard’s contingency model’, Journal of Applied Management and Entrepreneurship, 20(3), pp. 56–73.
Schein, E.H. (1996) ‘Three cultures of management: The key to organizational learning’, Sloan Management Review, 38(1), pp. 9–20.
Uhl-Bien, M., Riggio, R.E., Lowe, K.B. and Carsten, M.K. (2014) ‘Followership theory: A review and research agenda’, The Leadership Quarterly, 25(1), pp. 83–104.

responses.title: Task 2: Doing differently
responses.prompt:
Describe a situation in which the organisation you worked for performed in ways that could have been optimised.
What could have been done differently?
How might you have made a difference in that change?
A chance to describe how you would have led the team differently!
responses.responseText:
In the transformation to redesign collaboration structures and information governance, performance could have been improved by addressing structural conditions earlier rather than relying primarily on participatory leadership approaches. Progress was slowed by unclear decision ownership, diffuse authority, and inconsistent adoption across teams.

Situational and adaptive leadership approaches emphasise adjusting leadership style to context and engaging stakeholders (Meirovich and Gu, 2015). While useful, they were implicitly treated as sufficient mechanisms for alignment. This assumed that increased participation would resolve fragmentation. In practice, structural constraints were the primary limiting factor. Decision rights were not clearly defined, and teams operated with different assumptions about ownership and accountability.

This aligns with Schein’s (1996) argument that behaviour is shaped by underlying assumptions, and with Handy’s (1999) view that leadership cannot be separated from organisational context. Evidence from high-reliability environments further shows that clarity of roles and authority structures is critical for effective performance (Helmreich, 1987).

A more effective approach would have been to define decision authority and governance structures at the outset, clearly distinguishing consultative from directive processes. This would have required a more directive leadership role initially, establishing clear decision boundaries before opening participatory processes.
bibliography: Handy, C. (1999) Understanding Organizations. 4th edn. London: Penguin.
Helmreich, R.L. (1987) ‘The critical role of personality and organizational factors as determinants of reactions to restricted and stressful environments’. NASA Contractor Report NASA-CR-180621.
Meirovich, G. and Gu, J. (2015) ‘Empirical and theoretical validity of Hersey–Blanchard’s contingency model’, Journal of Applied Management and Entrepreneurship, 20(3), pp. 56–73.
Schein, E.H. (1996) ‘Three cultures of management: The key to organizational learning’, Sloan Management Review, 38(1), pp. 9–20.

responses.title: Task 1
responses.prompt: Develop your own working definition of coordination, then describe the characteristics that demonstrate effective coordination.
responses.responseText:
I understand coordination as the management of interdependence between actors operating in the same space. It may involve dividing tasks, negotiating access, resources, conditions and boundaries, sharing information and knowledge, and aligning or sequencing action, even where actors do not share the same priorities or final goals. Coordination may reduce fragmentation, but it remains fragile because actors continue to protect autonomy, access, legitimacy, resources and relative power (Grieco, 1988).

Although trust, respect and common understanding between actors are desirable, I accept that humanitarian coordination may also occur under mistrust, asymmetry and constraint. NGOs may work with states, militaries, donors, UN agencies, private companies or de facto authorities because these actors control access, funding, security, logistics, permissions or legitimacy, not because they share humanitarian goals (OCHA, 2015). It must therefore involve managing dependence without surrendering agency, preserving the line between being “coordinated with” others and being “coordinated by or for” their priorities (James, 2008).

I believe effective coordination should be understood by the kind of dependency being managed. Charles, McNulty and Pennell’s (1998) three-sector model is useful because it shows how different sectors combine distinct interests and resources, though effective coordination within these spaces also requires negotiating mandates, interests, red lines and workable terms of engagement (CCHN, 2019).

The actor and partnership map needs to make clear distinctions within and beyond the three sectors to include technical, digital, evidentiary, financial and knowledge-based dependencies. Digital systems and private technology actors can reshape authority, sovereignty and control (Martin et al., 2023). Commercial imagery affects what can be seen and evidenced (Wang et al., 2013). Starlink’s involvement in privately controlled connectivity infrastructure and hospitals in Gaza and Sudan (Townsend, 2024; Cartier, 2024), for example, shows such dependencies in crisis settings.

Knowledge and infrastructure contributors should also be included where they materially improve humanitarian capability. NASA’s Earthdata (2022) observations support crisis analysis around displacement, urban damage and refugee-settlement risks, while its VR training for astronaut preparation  (NASA, 2025) suggests useful lessons for NGO preparation in hostile environments. Meta Quest industrial safety simulations (2025) and telemedicine potential show a similar logic for training, remote support and decision-making in high-risk scenarios.

Funding is another coordination dependency: earmarking, reporting rules and eligibility criteria can lock agencies into donor priorities, even when coordination spaces identify different needs across the humanitarian-development gap (Hinds, 2015).

Effective coordination, in my view, is therefore proportionate rather than aimed at the highest possible level of integration. MSF illustrates this tension: even as a strongly independent medical actor, it depends on WASH, logistics, referrals, electricity, supply chains and access coordination (Spiegel, 2017), while still balancing the need to reject arrangements where medical priorities are redirected by military, state or donor agendas (OCHA, 2015).
bibliography: Cartier, C. (2024) ‘Musk activates internet service in Gaza hospital with help of UAE, Israel’, Reuters, 24 July. Available at: https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/musk-activates-internet-service-gaza-hospital-with-help-uae-israel-2024-07-24/ (Accessed: 6 May 2026).

responses.title: Task 2
responses.prompt:
Please start by reviewing the series of presented YouTube videos in the content with a critical eye. There are levels of bias/influence and perspective evident in each, and these need to be recognised. Ask yourself, "What is the message and agenda?" Why has the video been made? They are all different; some are very evidently from a particular perspective, others have subtler influences. The intention is to have you look past the face-message and consider the underlying intent. This is a critical analysis!
Pick at least two of the video case studies linked to from within the Session 5 content and explore how your working definition and characteristics might be applied in those situations.
responses.responseText:
Applying my definition, coordination should be judged not only by how actors work together, but by what interdependence is being managed and who controls its terms. Where aid movement depends on military, state or conflict-party control, the key issue is not just logistical flow, but humanitarian risk and who controls the conditions under which the coordination occurs. The MCDA Guidelines therefore frame my reading of Gaza and Syria: military and civil-defence support should remain exceptional, civilian-led and consistent with neutrality, impartiality and future humanitarian access (United Nations, 2006).

I interpret the Gaza video as framing coordination as a legitimacy claim by showing food, medical equipment and pharmaceutical products moving through a humanitarian coordination cell, suggesting that aid access is being managed (warinsouth, 2009). My reading is that this presents coordination as proof of access and safety, while leaving open who controls crossings, permissions, operating conditions, protection, military action and supply entry. Recent Guardian reporting on Gaza challenges the video's surface claim, with evidence of medical workers and aid-seeking civilians being detained, beaten and humiliated in Israeli detention, and Palestinians being killed while seeking food near aid distribution points (Kelly, Osman and Jallad, 2025; Beaumont, 2025). Coordination may therefore appear visible in the Gaza video, but whether aid reaches recipients remains unanswered, as does the wider question of what conditions are being created beyond the frame, at crossings, distribution points, hospitals and other sites of civilian protection.

Syria shows coordination as negotiated permission with UNHCR describing severe need yet aid to besieged and hard-to-reach areas depends on agreement between fighting parties (New Europe, 2015). OCHA’s access guidance supports this reading because humanitarian access depends on engagement with actors able to provide, restrict or influence movement (OCHA, 2015).

Libya and the Philippines shift the analysis from access to visibility, legitimacy and logistics. Al Jazeera foregrounds Misurata’s publicised need, but also shows displaced people elsewhere without aid, water, food or medical support (Al Jazeera English, 2011). Coordination here means identifying neglected gaps, not only responding to the most visible crisis site. In the Philippines, Cooper frames the problem through delay, unmet need and government image-management (Cooper, 2013a), while his later defence frames media coverage as bearing witness to failure (Cooper, 2013b). Walter’s military video frames the same crisis through capability: ships, aircraft, water production and amphibious access to remote areas (Walter, n.d.).

The deeper absence across the videos is also important. Affected communities appear mainly as victims, crowds, patients or recipients, not as coordination actors. Local organisations, priority-setting processes, verification of need and decisions about when military, political or logistical involvement becomes too compromising are mostly hidden. This supports my definition: coordination is the management of interdependence between actors who control movement, information, legitimacy, logistics, protection and the conditions under which aid becomes possible.

responses.title: Task 1: New innovation
responses.prompt: From the series of videos and texts within the content of Session 7, what is the most striking (i.e. interesting, concerning or ‘mind-blowing’) example presented in the material? Why?
responses.responseText:
What struck me most was the pattern behind the disaster robotics and AIDR examples. They reminded me of a Field Information Management Officer colleague whose Teams status reads: "'We’re not in an information age anymore. We’re in the information management age.' - Chris Hardwick". This captures a recurring issue I saw in this week’s material: humanitarian innovation is increasingly about how information is collected, classified, verified and used.

Murphy’s disaster robotics example shows that the value of robots and drones lies less in their novelty than in their ability to extend situational awareness, for example by producing data on damage, access, infrastructure and risk to support operational decisions (Murphy, 2015). The example also suggests that technological innovation can create a further challenge: how to make sense of increasing volumes of operational data. AIDR develops the same logic through AI, using human and machine intelligence to classify crisis-related social media into categories such as needs and damage (Imran, 2014; Imran et al., 2014). These examples show that disaster settings create both information gaps and information overload.

The wider literature supports this interpretation. Sun, Bocchini and Davison (2020) argue that AI can support disaster decision-making by processing large data volumes, but not replace professional judgement. Arnold, Goldschmitt and Rigotti (2023) show that information overload can reduce decision quality. Bernardo et al. (2024) add that data only creates value when governed through quality, lifecycle and responsibility structures. For me, the striking point is that these technologies are only truly innovative if humanitarian actors can do something meaningful with the information they produce. Their value depends on whether data can be classified, verified, governed and translated into accountable operational decisions.

responses.title: Task 2: Technology and You
responses.prompt: Reflect on how accelerating technologies impact health and humanitarianism, as well as social issues more broadly. To the extent possible, try to match the examples provided (or others that you may be aware of) and your own professional experiences. Will any of these be used in your practice anytime soon?
responses.responseText:
I see very strong parallels between the module material and my own work on information and knowledge management transformation and governance. Across the examples, I perceive a recurring issue around whether new technologies are usable, appropriate and governed well enough to improve decisions. This mirrors my work designing structures, metadata, permissions, sensitivity controls and governance so information can be found, trusted and used.

Accelerating technologies can improve humanitarian access, particularly where geography, infrastructure or expertise are constrained. MSF’s telemedicine service shows that specialist expertise can support frontline clinicians in low-resource settings and provide educational value (Delaigue et al., 2018). I also see a useful parallel with space medicine, because both humanitarian response and spaceflight involve remote, resource-constrained settings where people may need to act without immediate specialist support. NASA’s Intelligent Medical Crew Assistant uses AI and AR or VR to support just-in-time medical training and procedural guidance where autonomy is required (NASA TechPort, 2026). This connects to my own experience using VR for physiology and anatomy learning at the International Space University.

The social risks are equally important. Chen (2019) warns that HUMTECH can prioritise novelty and widen power gaps. Mulder et al. (2016) show that crisis data is socially produced, meaning platforms and categories can exclude affected people. Banks (2013) argues that technology solutions should be built from the problem context rather than imposed from outside. In my practice, AI-assisted classification, sensitivity scanning and search may be used soon in information management, but only if supported by data governance, quality controls and user-centred design. Otherwise, technology risks creating faster confusion rather than better knowledge.
